title: The Brewing Control Chart
body: Lockhart (1957) related soluble solids in the cup to quality and is the origin of the Brewing Control Chart that plots TDS against extraction yield.
source: Lockhart, 1957 — The Soluble Solids in Beverage Coffee as an Index to Cup Quality

title: A new Coffee Brewing Control Chart
body: At UC Davis, Guinard, Frost, Batali and colleagues mapped sensory and consumer response across brew strength and extraction. Preference splits into two groups; attributes do not follow the classic chart as a single peak.
source: Guinard et al., J. Food Sci. 2023 — A new Coffee Brewing Control Chart

title: Brew temperature at fixed strength and extraction
body: At fixed TDS and extraction yield, 87 / 90 / 93 °C change little in the sensory profile of drip coffee. Temperature is a lever to reach extraction, not a taste button.
source: Batali, Ristenpart, Guinard, Sci. Rep. 2020

title: Roast level interacts with strength and extraction
body: Roast level changes how brew strength and extraction present in the cup. Darker roasts read heavier at the same TDS.
source: Frost, Ristenpart, Guinard, J. Food Sci. 2020

title: Two preference segments among black-coffee drinkers
body: Consumer tasting across the brewing chart finds two preference segments rather than one ideal zone.
source: Cotter, Batali, Ristenpart, Guinard, J. Food Sci. 2021

title: Systematically Improving Espresso
body: Too fine a grind can make espresso extraction uneven. Coarser grind and a lower dose often improve reproducibility. Sour and bitter together is an evenness problem, not a level problem.
source: Cameron et al., Matter 2020 — Systematically Improving Espresso

title: Moisture-controlled triboelectrification during grinding
body: Bean moisture controls static charge while grinding. A little water (RDT) reduces clumps and can raise espresso extraction.
source: Méndez Harper et al., Matter 2023

title: Water is the charge-control that changes extraction
body: Of the chemical strategies tried, only water (< 0.05 mL/g) changes extraction parameters. Dark roasts can gain 15 % or more concentration with RDT.
source: Méndez Harper, Hendon et al., arXiv 2312.03103

title: Colder beans grind finer and narrower
body: Colder roasted beans produce a finer, narrower particle-size distribution.
source: Uman et al., Sci. Rep. 2016

title: Dissolved cations in coffee extraction
body: Magnesium and calcium affect extraction of aroma compounds; bicarbonate buffers acidity. Water chemistry is not just TDS.
source: Hendon, Colonna-Dashwood, J. Agric. Food Chem. 2014

title: SCAA Water for Brewing Specialty Coffee
body: Target ranges for brewing water: TDS about 75–250 ppm, general hardness around 50–175 ppm as CaCO3, alkalinity around 40–75 ppm, pH 6.5–7.5, sodium under 30 ppm.
source: SCAA, Water for Brewing Specialty Coffee, 2009

title: SCA Coffee Value Assessment
body: The CVA describes coffee with fragrance, aroma, flavor, aftertaste, acidity, sweetness, mouthfeel and overall. Kohi's seven taste axes follow this vocabulary.

title: Coffee Taster's Flavor Wheel
body: The SCA / WCR flavor wheel and sensory lexicon (2016) is the shared vocabulary for tasting notes.
source: SCA / WCR Coffee Taster's Flavor Wheel, 2016

title: The Physics of Filter Coffee
body: Jonathan Gagné's Physics of Filter Coffee and Coffee ad Astra cover fines, percolation and water recipes as documented practice, not peer review.
source: Gagné, The Physics of Filter Coffee (2020); Coffee ad Astra

title: Water for Coffee
body: Colonna-Dashwood and Hendon's Water for Coffee is the reference book on brewing-water chemistry: hardness, alkalinity, and how they taste.
source: Colonna-Dashwood, Hendon — Water for Coffee (2015)

title: Multiscale extraction modelling
body: Moroney et al. model extraction in a packed bed of coffee, the physics behind why grind, dose and time trade off.
source: Moroney et al., Chem. Eng. Sci. 2015

title: Flow-induced erosion of fines
body: Fines migrate during filtration. Agitation and pour rate change the bed, which is why a stir is a more drastic move than a grind click.
source: Mo, Johnston, Navarini, Ellero, Phys. Fluids 2021

title: Degassing of roasted coffee
body: Roasted coffee degasses on a curve that depends on roast and grind. That is why a rest window exists, and why a coffee under five days off roast needs a longer bloom.
source: Smrke et al., J. Agric. Food Chem. 2018

title: The Coffee Compass
body: Barista Hustle's Coffee Compass: sour → finer or longer; bitter → coarser or shorter; weak → shorter ratio; strong and muddy → longer ratio. One variable at a time.
source: Barista Hustle — DIY Water Recipes Redux; The Coffee Compass

title: Starting temperature by roast (G3)
body: Filter: light 94–100 °C, medium 90–94 °C, dark 85–90 °C. Espresso a few degrees cooler. Decaf: −2 °C and one notch coarser. Temperature mainly reaches extraction (F3).
source: Kohi G3; F3 Batali 2020

title: TDS and extraction yield (G4)
body: Filter usually sits around 1.15–1.45 % TDS and 18–22 % extraction. Espresso 8–12 % TDS, same yield band. EY = TDS × beverage ÷ dose. What TDS and extraction yield mean is this arithmetic, not a taste score.
source: Kohi G4; SCAA Brewing Control Chart

title: Suggested correction rules (G7)
body: Sour and not bitter, short time: grind finer (under-extracted). Bitter and long: grind coarser. Thin body, axes otherwise fine: shorter ratio (more strength, same extraction). Sour and bitter together: do not move the grind; check water and distribution. Yield over 22 % with bitterness: shorter time or cooler water. A V60 that tastes sour is usually under-extracted: finer grind or hotter water, not more acidity.
source: Kohi G7; Coffee Compass; F6

title: Rest after roasting (G5)
body: Filter, light roast: commonly 7–21 days off roast. Espresso 10–30 days. Darker roasts degas faster. Freezing extends the window. A coffee needs to rest so CO2 stops blowing the bed apart.
source: Kohi G5
